steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Language agents are a new and emerging class of artificial intelligence (AI) systems that use large language models to interact with the world. They take the latest advances in LLMs and apply them to the existing field of agent design. Interestingly, this combination has benefits for both fields. On one side, LLMs have limited knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Language agents reduce these problems by connecting LLMs to internal memory and to environments, which grounds them in existing knowledge or in external observations. On the other side, traditional agents often need handcrafted rules or reinforcement learning, which makes it hard to generalize to new environments. Language agents use the commonsense priors in LLMs to adapt to new tasks, so they depend less on human annotation or on trial-and-error learning.

The earliest agents used LLMs to directly select or generate actions, but more recent agents also use them to reason, to plan, and to manage long-term memory, in order to make better decisions. This newest generation of cognitive language agents uses very sophisticated internal processes (Figure 1 C). But at the moment, individual works describe these processes with their own custom terminology (like 'tool use', 'grounding', 'actions'), and this makes it hard to compare different agents, to understand how they evolve over time, or to build new agents with clean and consistent abstractions.

To set up a conceptual framework that organizes these efforts, we draw parallels with two ideas from the history of computing and AI: production systems and cognitive architectures. Production systems produce a set of outcomes by applying rules iteratively. They started out as string manipulation systems, which is an analog of the problem LLMs solve, and later the AI community adopted them to define systems that are capable of complex, hierarchically structured behaviors. For this, they were put into cognitive architectures that specified the control flow for selecting, applying, and even generating new productions. We suggest that there is a meaningful analogy between production systems and LLMs: productions indicate possible ways to modify strings, and in the same way LLMs define a distribution over changes or additions to text. This also suggests that the controls from cognitive architectures that were used with production systems might be just as applicable for turning LLMs into language agents.

- The CoALA framework
  - Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA) for general purpose language agents
  - memory (working, long-term), action space (internal, external), decision-making (interactive loop of planning and execution)
  - expresses existing agents, points to underexplored directions
  - combines conceptual-architecture papers and empirical surveys: theory + organizing empirical work
- Plan of the paper
  - Sec 2 background; Sec 3 parallels; Sec 4 CoALA and survey; Sec 5 case study; Sec 6 actionable steps; Sec 7 open questions; Sec 8 conclusion
  - applied agent design: Sections 4-6

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Language agents are a new and emerging class of artificial intelligence (AI) systems that use large language models to interact with the world. They take the latest advances in LLMs and apply them to the existing field of agent design. Interestingly, this combination has benefits for both fields. On one side, LLMs have limited knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Language agents reduce these problems by connecting LLMs to internal memory and to environments, which grounds them in existing knowledge or in external observations. On the other side, traditional agents often need handcrafted rules or reinforcement learning, which makes it hard to generalize to new environments. Language agents use the commonsense priors in LLMs to adapt to new tasks, so they depend less on human annotation or on trial-and-error learning.

The earliest agents used LLMs to directly select or generate actions, but more recent agents also use them to reason, to plan, and to manage long-term memory, in order to make better decisions. This newest generation of cognitive language agents uses very sophisticated internal processes (Figure 1 C). But at the moment, individual works describe these processes with their own custom terminology (like 'tool use', 'grounding', 'actions'), and this makes it hard to compare different agents, to understand how they evolve over time, or to build new agents with clean and consistent abstractions.

To set up a conceptual framework that organizes these efforts, we draw parallels with two ideas from the history of computing and AI: production systems and cognitive architectures. Production systems produce a set of outcomes by applying rules iteratively. They started out as string manipulation systems, which is an analog of the problem LLMs solve, and later the AI community adopted them to define systems that are capable of complex, hierarchically structured behaviors. For this, they were put into cognitive architectures that specified the control flow for selecting, applying, and even generating new productions. We suggest that there is a meaningful analogy between production systems and LLMs: productions indicate possible ways to modify strings, and in the same way LLMs define a distribution over changes or additions to text. This also suggests that the controls from cognitive architectures that were used with production systems might be just as applicable for turning LLMs into language agents.

So we propose Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA), a conceptual framework for characterizing and designing general purpose language agents. CoALA organizes agents along three key dimensions: how they store information (split into working and long-term memories), their action space (split into internal and external actions), and their decision-making procedure (structured as an interactive loop with planning and execution). Using these three concepts (memory, action, and decision-making), we show that CoALA can neatly express a large body of existing agents and can identify underexplored directions for developing new ones. Several recent papers propose conceptual architectures for general intelligence or survey language models and agents empirically, while this paper combines elements of both: we propose a theoretical framework and we use it to organize diverse empirical work. This grounds our theory in existing practices and lets us identify short-term and long-term directions for future work.

The rest of the paper is planned as follows. First we introduce production systems and cognitive architectures (Section 2), and show how the recent developments in LLMs and language agents recapitulate these historical ideas (Section 3). Motivated by these parallels, Section 4 introduces the CoALA framework and uses it to survey existing language agents. Section 5 gives a deeper case study of several prominent agents. Section 6 suggests actionable steps for constructing future language agents, and Section 7 highlights open questions in the broader arc of cognitive science and AI. Section 8 concludes. Readers who are interested in applied agent design may want to prioritize Sections 4-6.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Language agents [1,2,3,4] are an emerging class of artificial intelligence (AI) systems that use large language models [5,6,7,8] to interact with the world. They apply the latest advances in LLMs to the existing field of agent design [9]. Interestingly, this synthesis offers benefits for both fields. On one hand, LLMs possess limited knowledge and reasoning capabilities, and language agents mitigate these issues by connecting LLMs to internal memory and environments, grounding them to existing knowledge or external observations. On the other hand, traditional agents often require handcrafted rules [10] or reinforcement learning [11], which makes generalization to new environments challenging [12]. Language agents leverage the commonsense priors present in LLMs to adapt to novel tasks, reducing the dependence on human annotation or trial-and-error learning.

While the earliest agents used LLMs to directly select or generate actions [13,14], more recent agents additionally use them to reason [15], plan [16,17], and manage long-term memory [18,19] to improve decision-making. This latest generation of cognitive language agents uses remarkably sophisticated internal processes (Figure 1 C). Today, however, individual works use custom terminology to describe these processes (such as 'tool use', 'grounding', 'actions'), which makes it difficult to compare different agents, understand how they evolve over time, or build new agents with clean and consistent abstractions.

To establish a conceptual framework organizing these efforts, we draw parallels with two ideas from the history of computing and artificial intelligence (AI): production systems and cognitive architectures. Production systems generate a set of outcomes by iteratively applying rules [20]. They originated as string manipulation systems (an analog of the problem that LLMs solve) and were subsequently adopted by the AI community to define systems capable of complex, hierarchically structured behaviors [21]. To do so, they were incorporated into cognitive architectures that specified control flow for selecting, applying, and even generating new productions [22,23,24]. We suggest a meaningful analogy between production systems and LLMs: just as productions indicate possible ways to modify strings, LLMs define a distribution over changes or additions to text. This suggests that controls from cognitive architectures used with production systems might be equally applicable to transforming LLMs into language agents.

We therefore propose Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA), a conceptual framework to characterize and design general purpose language agents. CoALA organizes agents along three key dimensions: their information storage (divided into working and long-term memories); their action space (divided into internal and external actions); and their decision-making procedure (structured as an interactive loop with planning and execution). Through these three concepts (memory, action, and decision-making), we show that CoALA can neatly express a large body of existing agents and identify underexplored directions for developing new ones. While several recent papers propose conceptual architectures for general intelligence [27,28] or empirically survey language models and agents [29,1,2], this paper combines elements of both: we propose a theoretical framework and use it to organize diverse empirical work. This grounds our theory in existing practices and allows us to identify both short-term and long-term directions for future work.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We first introduce production systems and cognitive architectures (Section 2) and show how recent developments in LLMs and language agents recapitulate these historical ideas (Section 3). Motivated by these parallels, Section 4 introduces the CoALA framework and uses it to survey existing language agents. Section 5 provides a deeper case study of several prominent agents. Section 6 suggests actionable steps to construct future language agents, while Section 7 highlights open questions in the broader arc of cognitive science and AI. Finally, Section 8 concludes. Readers interested in applied agent design may prioritize Sections 4-6.
